analysis.one_liner: Creates a voluntary Medicare prescription drug benefit covering seniors' outpatient medications.
analysis.headline: Sen. Bob Graham introduced the Medicare drug benefit bill with 30 Senate Democrats as cosponsors in June 2002; the Senate Finance Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a prescription drug benefit to Medicare starting in 2004. Seniors who enrolled would pay a $25 monthly premium and fixed copays — $10 for generics, $40 for preferred brand-name drugs, $60 for other brand-name drugs — with no deductible, and no cost-sharing at all once out-of-pocket drug costs reached $4,000 in a year. It also provided extra help for low-income beneficiaries, subsidized employers who kept retiree drug coverage, and delivered the benefit through private plans chosen by competitive bidding.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who lack drug coverage and pay retail prices out of pocket. Roughly 40 million seniors and disabled beneficiaries would have gained access to negotiated prices, fixed copays, and a $4,000 annual out-of-pocket cap, with extra assistance for low-income beneficiaries. Employers with retiree drug plans would also have received federal subsidies to keep that coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors paying out of pocket for prescriptions

how_it_helps.text: The benefit would cover outpatient prescription drugs with no deductible and fixed copays of $10 for generics, $40 for preferred brand-name drugs, and $60 for nonpreferred brand-name drugs.

Beneficiaries would pay nothing in cost-sharing once their out-of-pocket drug costs reached $4,000 in a year, and plans would have to give beneficiaries access to the negotiated prices used for payment.
The monthly premium for 2004 was set at $25, with later increases tied to program spending growth.
The bill provided additional cost-sharing assistance for low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
An Employer Incentive Program would pay sponsors two-thirds of the government contribution for retirees who keep qualifying employer drug coverage instead of enrolling in the new benefit.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through annual Treasury appropriations covering program costs that exceed the $25 monthly premiums, deposited in a dedicated Prescription Drug Account in the Medicare trust fund. Beneficiaries enrolled in the program would bear premiums and copays; pharmacies and drug-plan middlemen would bear new contracting, auditing, and price-reporting requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a large new open-ended entitlement: each year Treasury must appropriate whatever benefits and administrative costs exceed premium collections, with no overall spending cap.

The benefit is delivered through private 'eligible entities' — pharmacy benefit management companies, insurers, and pharmacy systems that bid for contracts and receive management payments — rather than administered directly by Medicare, adding a layer of private administration to a public benefit.

The design relies on competitive bidding among private entities to hold down prices rather than direct negotiation with drug manufacturers, so savings depend on how well that bidding works — something the bill itself directs the GAO to study.
Even after the benefit, a beneficiary with heavy drug use would still pay up to $4,000 a year out of pocket before coverage became fully free, and copays rise with drug price inflation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors without drug coverage, the benefit is substantial: no deductible, predictable copays, negotiated prices, and a hard cap on annual out-of-pocket costs. The honest costs are fiscal — an uncapped new federal entitlement — and structural, since the money flows through private plan middlemen whose management fees and bidding behavior determine how much of the public money reaches beneficiaries as lower prices. A taxpayer who prefers direct government negotiation might fairly call the design a compromise.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced; the committee took no action on it, and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Graham introduced the Medicare Outpatient Prescription Drug Act of 2002 on June 14, 2002, joined by 30 Senate Democrats as cosponsors and no Republicans.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.

No further action appears in the record after two sets of sponsor introductory remarks; the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or House action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, private plan middlemen, insurers, and brand-name drug makers avoided a Medicare drug benefit built on competitive bidding and negotiated prices; seniors without drug coverage kept paying full retail prices for prescriptions for another year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private drug-plan middlemen and drug makers

for.name: Sen. Bob Graham
for.role: U.S. Senator from Florida; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor twice.

for.name: 30 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Senate Majority Leader and other party leaders.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Medicare legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 14, 2002 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Advanced his own competing approach to a Medicare drug benefit during the 2002 debate rather than backing the Graham bill.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and health insurers
against.role: Industries affected by Medicare drug benefit design
against.what_they_did: Opposed drug benefit designs featuring government price pressure during the 2002 debate, favoring coverage delivered entirely through private plans.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Democrats; the bill drew no Republican cosponsors in a Senate split 49 Democrats to 49 Republicans.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: The bill would make private entities — including pharmacy benefit management companies, insurers, and pharmacy systems — the permanent delivery channel for a new public drug benefit, paying them to manage and administer coverage chosen through competitive bidding. Beneficiaries get the coverage, but a layer of private middlemen is locked in as its gatekeeper.

A new Medicare drug benefit would greatly expand the pool of paying customers, but the bill requires plans to give beneficiaries access to negotiated prices and relies on competitive bidding, which pressures drug prices. Manufacturers had a stake in a benefit design without that price pressure.
Pharmacies that join the program are guaranteed a reasonable dispensing fee, cannot refuse to dispense covered drugs to beneficiaries, and are barred from charging more than the negotiated price.
The Employer Incentive Program subsidizes two-thirds of the government contribution for each retiree kept on a qualifying employer drug plan, encouraging companies to maintain retiree coverage.
The bill revises Medicare supplemental insurance benefit packages and eliminates obsolete policies with no grandfathering, forcing existing Medigap drug coverage to conform to the new program.
